summary: Specifies the "tel" URI scheme, which identifies resources by telephone number. It makes a phone number usable as a link. It obsoletes RFC 2806.

plainLanguage.summary: A tel URI writes a telephone number in a form that other programs can recognize. It names the number, but does not tell a device how to dial it.

questions: how to write a phone number as a uri

tel uri global vs local number
how to add an extension to a tel uri
subtitle: How to write a telephone number as a URI, global or local, without specifying how to dial it.

tldr.problem: Programs need a consistent way to identify a telephone number without encoding the dialing steps needed on a particular phone or network.
tldr.mechanism: The tel: scheme identifies a number in global form or, when that is not possible, local form with a phone-context parameter. Optional parameters can identify an extension or ISDN subaddress.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3966 replaces RFC 2806 and is updated by RFC 5341. A tel URI identifies a number; it does not specify how to place the call.

today: RFC 3966 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2806 and is updated by RFC 5341.

sections.title: A Number Is Not a Dialing Plan
sections.content:
RFC 3966 defines the tel URI, a way to identify a resource by its telephone number. The number can refer to a point in a public or private telephone network or on the Internet, and does not identify a particular physical device.

The URI identifies a canonical number, not a dial string: the digits, symbols, pauses, or tones a user enters. A phone or gateway can turn the number into the actions needed on its network. The URI also does not specify whether a call is voice, fax, or data.
sections.plainLanguage: A tel URI names a telephone number. A separate dialing system decides what actions are needed to reach it.

sections.title: The URI Form
sections.content:
A tel URI begins with tel: and then contains a global or local number. A global number starts with +. The number may use hyphens, full stops, or parentheses as visual separators; spaces MUST NOT be used as separators.

Parameters follow the number after semicolons. This specification defines phone-context, isub, and ext. A parameter, extension, subaddress, or context MUST NOT appear more than once. If present, an extension or subaddress comes first, then the context, then other parameters in alphabetical order.

The reserved characters +, ;, =, and ? MUST NOT be percent-encoded when they divide URI parts. They MUST be percent-encoded when they occur inside parameter values.
sections.plainLanguage: A tel URI starts with tel:, followed by a number and any labelled details. Dashes and dots help people read the number, but spaces are not allowed as separators.

sections.title: When Two tel URIs Match
sections.content:
Two tel URIs are equivalent only if both numbers are global or both are local. Their digits must match after visual separators are removed. Their parameters must also match by name; a parameter present in only one URI makes them different.

A domain-name phone context is compared as a host name. A global-number context is compared digit by digit after removing visual separators. Comparison is case-insensitive, but parameter names and values SHOULD use lower case because some systems compare them case-sensitively.
sections.plainLanguage: To compare two tel URIs, ignore number separators and compare the digits and parameters. If one URI has an extra parameter, the two are different.

sections.title: Global Numbers and Local Context
sections.content:
Numbers MUST use global form unless they cannot be represented that way. A global number starts with + and follows the country and national number rules in E.123 and E.164. Implementations MUST NOT assume that numbers have a fixed, minimum, or maximum length.

A private number, emergency number, or service code may need local form. A local number MUST have a phone-context that identifies where the number is unique. The context can be a global number or its leading digits, or a domain name controlled by the entity managing the context. It does not turn the local number into an E.164 number by simply adding digits.

Alphabetic keypad spellings are not supported because the mapping from letters to digits is not uniform internationally.
sections.plainLanguage: Use a global number when one exists. A local number needs a context, such as a company domain, so a reader knows where that number is unique.

sections.title: Extensions and Other Parameters
sections.content:
The isub parameter carries an ISDN subaddress. The ext parameter identifies a station behind a non-ISDN PBX. A URI may contain one of these parameters, but MUST NOT contain both.

Future extensions may add mandatory or optional parameters. A parameter whose name starts with m- is mandatory: an implementation MUST NOT use the URI if it does not understand that parameter. An implementation MAY ignore an unknown optional parameter, and a forwarding entity MUST NOT remove or change an optional parameter it does not understand.
sections.plainLanguage: Parameters add details such as an extension. If a detail is marked mandatory and a program does not understand it, the program must not use the URI.

sections.title: Using tel URIs in Web Pages and SIP
sections.content:
An HTML link SHOULD show the telephone number as its link text so a person can tell what the link will do. On a public page, the URI SHOULD use a global number even if the visible number is formatted locally.

SIP can carry a tel URI in places where it accepts a URI. Unless a user agent connects directly to a PSTN gateway, a SIP proxy generally translates the tel URI into a SIP URI that points to a gateway. A proxy MUST NOT translate a local-number URI if it does not understand its context. If it cannot find a route for the context, it returns 404 (Not Found).

A dial plan in the end system translates a user's dial string into a tel or SIP URI. The RFC keeps the tel scheme separate from SIP because the number can be reached by different signaling and gateway methods.
sections.plainLanguage: A web link should show the number it names. In a SIP network, a proxy can use that number and its context to find a route to a gateway.

sections.title: Consent Before Placing a Call
sections.content:
A web client or similar tool MUST NOT place a call from a tel URI without the user's explicit consent. An unwanted call may cost money, occupy a phone line, or expose an unlisted caller number that can be linked to other information.

An HTML link can hide its actual telephone target behind misleading text. A tel URI can also expose a phone number, and its scheme prefix may make the number easier to find with a search engine.
sections.plainLanguage: A program must ask before a tel link places a call. A hidden or unexpected number can cause charges or reveal the caller's number.
